copycopy_graph.py --source-env <neo4j_env> --target-env <target_env> (add-on I), then module_tags.py check and modules, release_record.py write and check when this load has records, and model_review.py therethe target's graph hash equals the source's and the report's, the tags check passes there, the records read back, and no ERROR finding
jenathe jena dataset, emptied, then rdfstore.py roundtrip of the data files and their release graphs (files mode: each file under its graph name)the store's export has the files' RDFC-1.0 hash
explorethe explore_fuseki dataset, emptied and loaded with the data and inferred.nt, then explore.py compare against the local graph and, when this run copied, against the targetevery saved walk and the module map give the same edges, nodes and tags in Neo4j and in Jena
rebuildsee belowthe store's export hashes equal to the release, the rebuild's triples and graph hashes equal this run's, and its own load, tags, release records, copy and walks pass

The rebuild#

rebuild proves the graph can be rebuilt from a store's copy alone. It needs project and load to have run into out (in this run or an earlier one), with the inputs run-manifest.json records. It loads the same local Neo4j again: load_verify.py empties it first, and the equal graph hashes prove the rebuilt graph is the one the first load verified.

  1. With source jena, it exports everything the store holds (rdfstore.py export --ttl-dir), packs the release files the same way the round trip did, and requires equal RDFC-1.0 hashes (rdfstore.py compare). A rebuild from Jena loads Jena first when this run hasn't. With repo, it takes the repository files.
  2. It maps the exported graphs to the inputs. A data file maps to the graph named by its owl:versionIRI (in files mode, by its graph name), and a release graph's shapes file to <version IRI>/<name>. A shape file that is no release graph, such as a whole-graph shapes file, was never in the store, so it comes from the repository, and the run says which.
  3. It runs project and load into rebuild.out, then requires loadable.nt and inferred.nt to hold the first run's triples, compared as RDF 1.1 terms, and both reports to hold exactly determinism_hash_sorted and determinism_hash_shuffled, non-empty and equal to the first run's. A store export may write a literal typed xsd:string as a plain literal, which RDF 1.1 defines as the same term, so the files need not be byte-equal. The equal graph hashes prove Neo4j holds the same graph.
  4. It tags, writes the release records (releases mode), copies when target_env is set (with replace_target), and explores when queries is set.

run_projection.py compare-triples <rebuild out> <baseline out> and compare-reports <rebuild report> <baseline report> run step 3's two checks on their own.

What it leaves behind#

The run starts no server and stops none. The local Neo4j holds the last load (after a rebuild, the rebuilt graph, which has the same hash), the target holds the copy, the jena dataset holds the release, and the explore_fuseki and triplestore_fuseki datasets hold what their steps loaded. A Fuseki dataset started with --mem empties when its server stops. To empty a Neo4j database, delete only what the run loaded.

Add-ons and anti-patterns#

From references/add-ons.md

Read it when a consumer asks for something the core pipeline does not give (superclass labels, split language keys, exact decimals, units, provenance, business keys, a GRAPH TYPE, the graph on a server without plugins, the same data in a triple store or in Databricks), or when reviewing a projection.

Add-ons (adopt only when needed, and record each)#

Add-onUse whenWhat to add
A. Superclass labelsMATCH (:lib_Item) should find copies without walking the hierarchyThe reason step with --include-indirect true already loads every inferred superclass as a label (pipeline.md, rule 4); adopt this add-on only to leave out upper-ontology roots
B. Language policyLabels in several languageslpg:langPolicy "splitKeys", giving label_en, label_fr
C. Exact decimalsFines, fees, anything computed with exact arithmeticlpg:cypherType "STRING" on xsd:decimal properties
D. Known exclusionsOWL axioms you will not projectList them in exclusions.nt; the round-trip diff ignores them
E. UnitsQuantities with unitsQUDT value and unit pattern, not custom datatypes
F. Module tags, the module graph and the walkSeveral packages (modules) in one graph, and people want to see which module each fact came from, or walk any node across modules in Neo4j and a triple storemodule_tags.py tag and check, module_tags.py modules, explore.py and the files in queries/ (see below)
G. Business keysConsumers MERGE on a key such as a barcodelpg:keyProperty true, giving an extra uniqueness constraint
H. A GRAPH TYPEThe target runs Neo4j Enterprise 2026.02 or later and should reject data outside the modelbuild.py graph-type --output graph-type.cypher (see below)
I. Copy to another Neo4jThe graph must live on a server that has no n10s or APOC, in a database you namecopy_graph.py (see below)
J. A triple storeSPARQL consumers need the same dataThe rdf-store skill loads the files and proves the round trip; triplestore.py (see below) adds the counts against the n10s export
K. DatabricksThe data must also live in Unity CatalogThe rdf-store skill: a Delta table of quads, written and read by a notebook's own Spark session (SparkStore), with the same round trip through a staging table. It runs in the notebook, not from run_projection.py: see multi-store.md and the rdf-store skill's references/stores.md
L. A Data Modeling MCP modelReviewers want an Arrows drawing or a Mermaid diagram of the graphbuild.py data-model (see below)
M. Release recordsPeople reading the graph must see which release of each module it holds, whether it passed, and which rules loaded itrelease_record.py (see below)

F. Module tags, the module graph and the walk#

Use it when one graph holds several released packages, as a modular ontology does. Run it after step 6 (and again on a copy, add-on I), against the package files the projection loaded:

  1. Tag. module_tags.py tag --config <config> (--uri U | --env E) [--inferred inferred.nt] [--separator _] <package.ttl>... sets the reserved property graph on every :Resource node and every relationship between two of them: the package's owl:versionIRI, the same IRI the rdf-store skill names that package's named graph by, so Neo4j and the triple store name modules alike. The rules are read from the package files, never from the graph: a node takes the package that types it (else the packages that mention it), preferring the package whose ontology IRI starts the node's IRI, then the first in dependency order; a relationship takes the first package in dependency order whose file holds the triple; an inferred triple takes its subject's tag. graph is never a SHORTEN key (those always carry a prefix and the separator), and load_verify.graph_hash leaves it out, so tagging keeps the report's hash and copy_graph.py still compares equal and copies the tags. tag fails (exit 1) when the graph holds a node or relationship no package states.
  2. Check. module_tags.py check (same arguments) is the no-loss check for the tags: every node and relationship carries exactly one graph, equal to the package it came from, and every expected node and edge is in the graph. Run it on the local graph and on every copy.
  3. The module graph. module_tags.py modules (--uri U | --env E) [--separator _] <package.ttl>... writes one (:Module {uri, ontology, version}) per package and (:Module)-[:REQUIRES {pin}]->(:Module) per dcterms:requires, pointing at the release loaded, with the version the package pins as pin: a pin older than the loaded release is a requirement that lags. :Module nodes carry no :Resource label, so the projection's hash and checks never see them; copy_graph.py does not copy them, so run modules on each target. The projection itself already holds each package's owl:Ontology header node and its dcterms:requires links, but those point at bare version-IRI nodes, not at the loaded modules; the module graph joins them. module_tags.py construct --output <file> writes the same graph as a SPARQL CONSTRUCT over a store with one named graph per package (queries/module-map.rq), each requirement its own node so a pin stays with the package that names it.
  4. The walk. explore.py walk --config <config> (--uri U | --env E) --sparql <query URL> --iri <IRI> [--hops N] [--separator _] returns, from Neo4j and from the store, every relationship within N hops of the node (default 2), both directions, with its predicate and module tag, and every node it reaches with its tag, and says whether the two answers are equal. It reads hop by hop, so Neo4j and SPARQL ask the same question; on the store side the tags are derived from the named graphs by the rules of step 1, so agreement also proves the tags. explore.py compare ... --queries <queries.json> [--report <json>] runs a project's saved walks ({"queries": [{"name", "iri", "hops"}]}; named shortcuts such as "a process across modules" are walks from that kind of node) and compares the module map too. n10s's schema relationships (n4sch_SCO, SPO, DOMAIN, RANGE, EQC and the *_RESTRICTION types, some pointing at a restriction's filler) are derived from the ontology, not package triples: module_tags.py tags each with the tag of the node it starts from and checks that, and the walk leaves them out, since the triples they repeat are ordinary relationships too. Load the projection's inferred.nt into the store as its own named graph, urn:ontology-to-lpg:inferred unless --inferred-graph names another; a triple in any other graph that is not a package shows as a difference, never silently dropped. When the load renamed the graph's names (pipeline.md, rule 11), give tag, check, modules, walk and compare the same --separator: it is how each reads a type back into its predicate and tells the schema relationships (n4sch plus the separator) apart; a prefix that holds the separator is refused before any query.
  5. Exploring by hand. queries/walk.cypher (rows, with tags) and queries/walk-visual.cypher (paths to see; colour nodes by graph) paste into Neo4j Browser, or save as a Browser favourite or a Bloom search phrase with $iri; queries/walk-2-hops.rq pastes into Fuseki's query page (set the start in VALUES; explore.py sparql-walk --hops N --output <file> writes it for another hop limit); queries/module-map.cypher and queries/module-map.rq show the module graph. The two Cypher walks name n10s's schema prefix in their WHERE line; for a graph loaded with another separator, change it as their comments say. On one modular ontology on 2026-10-25, the walk's single-query forms returned the same 2,181 edges as explore.py. Two hops from a node reach a class node such as skos:Concept, and from there every node of that class, so a walk of two hops is often wide: use the module tags to read it, or one hop to stay close.

Plain RDF files work too (run_projection.py's files mode, run-config.md): module_tags.py --graph FILE=IRI makes a file with no owl:versionIRI a package named by its graph, with no requirements, and explore.py --files reads every graph in the store the same way.

H. A GRAPH TYPE from the shapes#

In the validation map (multi-store.md) this is G1 to G4.

build.py graph-type --config <config> --shapes <shapes>... --output graph-type.cypher [--separator _] <data>... writes one CYPHER 25 ALTER CURRENT GRAPH TYPE SET { ... } statement to the file, each left-out item as a quoted // left out: comment, and prints only the quoted file name and counts. It stops (exit 2) when the shapes give no element type at all. The Cypher manual marks the statement "Cypher 25 only", Enterprise Edition, introduced in Neo4j 2026.02 (https://neo4j.com/docs/cypher-manual/current/schema/graph-types/set-graph-types/; the element syntax is at https://neo4j.com/docs/cypher-manual/current/schema/syntax/). It emits:

  • one node element type per sh:targetClass that has at least one typed property, (:Label => {prop :: TYPE ...}), with a typed property for each property shape on a value whose sh:datatype maps to a Cypher type (design-rules.md, the XSD table). The property is LIST<TYPE NOT NULL> exactly when the load stores it as an array, which is the load script's own multivalued list (pipeline.md, rule 10: global per predicate, so sh:maxCount 1 on one class does not make it a scalar where another class or the data makes it a list), and a scalar otherwise; that is why the command reads the data files. It is NOT NULL when sh:minCount is at least 1, list or scalar (a hosted Enterprise database accepted LIST<STRING NOT NULL> NOT NULL on 2026-10-23). A target with no typed property gets no node element type: that server rejected an empty one ((:Label =>) and => {} were both syntax errors), while a relationship endpoint may name a label that has no element type of its own;
  • one relationship element type per predicate whose property shapes name one sh:class, (:Source)-[:TYPE =>]->(:Target).

When two property shapes on one target map the same key differently, the first (by shape IRI) is kept and the other listed; a property shape with both sh:datatype and sh:class is typed as a property and its relationship listed.

It leaves out, and lists as // left out: comments: relationship counts, sh:in, sh:pattern, sh:nodeKind, ranges and lengths (no GRAPH TYPE form), property shapes with no mappable datatype or class, and paths that are not a predicate. Labels and types are the kept graph's names, backtick-quoted: n10s's, or with --separator the ones the load renamed them to (pipeline.md, rule 11), so the statement names the elements that exist. On neo4j:2026.06 Community (2026.06.0, 2026-10-23), the library statement passed the parser and was refused with 51N27 'ALTER CURRENT GRAPH TYPE SET' is not supported in community edition, while a misspelt type (STRNG) was refused as a syntax error; On a hosted Enterprise database on 2026-10-23, on one multi-module test ontology, the statement held 35 node and 46 relationship element types after the two fixes above (no empty node types; list types from the load's multivalued list). It was accepted (SHOW CURRENT GRAPH TYPE returned it), a write with an integer where the type declared a string was rejected with Neo.ClientError.Schema.ConstraintValidationFailed, and ALTER CURRENT GRAPH TYPE SET {} cleared it. Coverage depends on sh:targetClass shapes: a shape that targets with sh:targetNode or SHACL-SPARQL gives no element type. Apply it after the load and the verify step, never instead of them: the n10s shapes and the round trip stay the gate.

Applying it (G2 to G4 in multi-store.md): after the copy of add-on I (V13), run the file's statement on the target as one statement (with cypher-shell -f graph-type.cypher, or a driver), then CYPHER 25 SHOW CURRENT GRAPH TYPE must return it. Then probe: in a transaction, write a value that breaks one declared property type (for example an integer where the type says STRING); the write must fail with Neo.ClientError.Schema.ConstraintValidationFailed; roll the transaction back. A refused statement means the statement is wrong, not the data, which passed V6 to V13. From then on the database refuses such writes from any application, where n10s cannot run. CYPHER 25 ALTER CURRENT GRAPH TYPE SET {} clears it. The Neo4j skill neo4j-cypher-skill, references/graph-type.md, has the full syntax.

I. Copy to another Neo4j#

n10s and APOC run only where the projection is built: "neosemantics is only available for Neo4j self-hosted (CE and EE)" (https://neo4j.com/labs/neosemantics/, "Availability & Installation"), and a managed or shared server often allows no plugin. So build and verify locally (steps 5 and 6), then copy the verified graph with plain Cypher to a database you name:

uv run --no-project --with rdflib --with neo4j python3 copy_graph.py \
  --source-env <local.env> [--source-database <name>] \
  --target-env <target.env> [--target-database <name>] \
  --report projection-report.json [--replace] [--batch 1000] [--query-timeout 120]

On Windows, after py -m pip install rdflib neo4j, the same line starts py copy_graph.py.

Run it after check-report passed and before anything else writes to the local graph (running.md, rule 5, step 3). Each env file holds NEO4J_URI, NEO4J_USERNAME, NEO4J_PASSWORD and optionally NEO4J_DATABASE; keep both outside the repository. --source <URI> with NEO4J_PASSWORD and NEO4J_USERNAME in the environment replaces --source-env. --source-database and --target-database name the database on each side and override the file's NEO4J_DATABASE; without either the server's default database is used. The script never prints a password.

  • No plugin on the target. The script sends the target plain Cypher only: CALL db.info(), a node count, the uniqueness constraint on :Resource(uri), UNWIND batches with dynamic labels and types, and the two reads of the graph hash. It calls no n10s or APOC procedure on either server. test_engine_gate.py pins the exact statements against a stand-in target that refuses any plugin call.
  • What it copies. Every :Resource node with its labels and properties (the n4sch__ schema nodes included) and every relationship between two :Resource nodes. It leaves out n10s's configuration nodes (_GraphConfig, _NsPrefDef, _n10sValidatorConfig).
  • No separator. It takes no --separator: it copies every label, relationship type and property key as it is and compares whole-graph hashes, so a graph the load renamed (pipeline.md, rule 11) copies like any other. The tag check, the module graph and the review you run on the copy take the flag.
  • Only the verified graph. --report is required: the script reads it before touching either database and stops (exit 2) unless the report earns its pass, which it rechecks rather than trusting passed (every field check-report checks except the fingerprints: the numbers, equal hashes, compiled rows each with a passing case, the mutant). It also stops on an unknown flag (such as the old --expect-hash). Then it stops (exit 1), before it writes or deletes anything on the target, unless the source's graph hash equals the report's determinism_hash_sorted.
  • Never onto the source. Before it writes or deletes anything it asks both sides for their database id (CALL db.info()) and stops (exit 1) when they are the same database, whatever URI, host alias or scheme reached it. Two databases of one server have two ids, so a copy from one to the other is allowed.
  • A target that holds nodes. It refuses a target that holds any node unless --replace is given, which deletes everything in that database first, in batches. So --replace can only ever install the verified graph.
  • The proof. After the copy it hashes the target as load_verify.py does (pipeline.md, rule 17) and fails unless it equals the source's. A failure during the copy can leave a partial graph on the target; the script says so, and a rerun with --replace replaces it.

Since the graph hash writes a date (or any non-JSON value) with its type, a report written before that change for a graph holding such values no longer matches: rerun load_verify.py to write a current report before copying. README.md, "Status", gives the tested copies.

rdflib-neo4j (https://neo4j.com/labs/rdflib-neo4j/) is the Neo4j Labs alternative: an RDFLib store backed by Neo4j, "a client-side alternative to Neosemantics for cloud-native Neo4j deployments". It loads RDF from the client but does not run the in-graph SHACL, the round trip or the hash of steps 5 and 6, so this skill copies a graph those steps verified instead.

J. The same files in a triple store#

Loading a store and proving that nothing was lost (an export of everything the store holds, compared with the source by its RDFC-1.0 hash) is the rdf-store skill, split out of this one on 2026-10-24; use it for every triple store and for the Databricks table. What stays here is triplestore.py, the count check that ties a store to the projection: its three-way counts compare the files, the store and the n10s export.

triplestore.py loads the validated inputs into any SPARQL 1.1 store and checks per-graph and per-predicate counts, and with a projection report the three-way counts. It speaks only W3C protocols: the SPARQL 1.1 Graph Store HTTP Protocol (https://www.w3.org/TR/sparql11-http-rdf-update/) to replace each named graph with PUT (?graph=<IRI>), and the SPARQL 1.1 Protocol to count. There is no store-specific code.

uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 triplestore.py --gsp <graph store URL> --query <SPARQL URL> \
  [--env <store.env>] [--graph-base <IRI>] --inferred inferred.nt \
  [--projection-report projection-report.json] [--cq <question.rq>]... --report triplestore-report.json <data.ttl>...
  • Graphs: one named graph per input file: the owl:versionIRI of its one owl:Ontology, else that ontology's IRI, else <graph-base><file name>; inferred.nt goes to <graph-base>inferred. The default base is urn:lpg-projection:graph:; pick one under your own domain for anything shared.
  • Credentials: --env names a file that may set SPARQL_GSP, SPARQL_QUERY, SPARQL_USER and SPARQL_PASSWORD (HTTP Basic); flags win. The password is never printed. The report stores the endpoints redacted (shell.redact: all userinfo before @ and the value of a credential-like query key such as sig or key become ***). Every error, in setup or in a request, prints a fixed context and the exception's type (and an HTTP status), never its text, and a refusal holds no text the user supplied (no path, value or unknown option; an unverified projection report gets a count of failed checks, which build.py check-report lists), because any of them can carry a URL or a credential (shell.error_line, shell.Refusal).
  • Counts: a count is the number of distinct triples; blank nodes count as triples, without matching labels. Per graph, COUNT(*) must equal the file's triples; per predicate, the distinct triples over all the loaded graphs must equal the files' together; with --projection-report, they must also equal the report's export_predicate_counts, the n10s export with the schema rows left out (n10s's configuration nodes are never exported). That is the three-way check: files, store and graph.
  • The projection report is rechecked: --projection-report must earn its pass (the same recheck as add-on I), not only say passed: true.
  • The report is fail-closed: the report named by --report, and its .failed file, are deleted before anything else; the report is written, by a rename, only when every count matched. A mismatch writes the details to <report>.failed; a failed request writes nothing.
  • Competency questions: each --cq SPARQL SELECT runs over the loaded graphs (as default-graph-uri parameters) and its row count goes into the report.

Start the store as the rdf-store skill's references/stores.md says: the plain Apache download, jena-fuseki-server-6.2.0.jar (SHA-256 2c92c598e65ab69d99820052e05f4277ed1d77980a8845f87545ad35b71a76ee), started with java -jar jena-fuseki-server-6.2.0.jar --mem --update --localhost --port 3030 /ds. Then --gsp http://127.0.0.1:3030/ds --query http://127.0.0.1:3030/ds/query.

It exits 0 when every count matches, 1 on a mismatch or a failed request, 2 on bad input. Fuseki 6.2.0 refused a urn:x- graph name as a relative IRI, which is why the default base has no x- namespace. README.md, "Status", gives the tested runs. The export and the comparison with the source (multi-store.md, hop 3) are the rdf-store skill's round trip.

L. The graph as a Data Modeling MCP model#

build.py data-model --config <config> --shapes <shapes>... --output data-model.json [--separator _] <data>... writes the shapes' element types (build.element_types, the mapping add-on H also reads) as a DataModel of the Neo4j Data Modeling MCP server, mcp-neo4j-data-modeling 0.8.2 (https://github.com/neo4j-contrib/mcp-neo4j, servers/mcp-neo4j-data-modeling, data_model.py at commit 0eaf613e0f). One node per label a shape targets or a relationship reaches, keyed on uri; one property per typed key, with a list typed LIST and its element type in the description; one relationship per source, key and target, every label pair kept. Labels and types are the kept graph's names (--separator as for add-on H). It holds more than the GRAPH TYPE: a label with no typed property and a relationship type used between several label pairs stay in the model, and add-on H drops both. metadata.left_out lists what the shapes give no typed form; metadata.not_in_graph_type lists what the model holds and a GRAPH TYPE cannot; add-on H's comments are exactly the two lists together. Before it writes, the command checks the model against that server's DataModel under strict validation (build.data_model_problems; test_modeling.py checks it against the pinned package on every case) and exits 1 on a problem.

Give the file's JSON to the server's tools: validate_data_model (it accepted the library model on 2026-10-24), then get_mermaid_config_str or export_to_arrows_json for Arrows.app. Leave out its export_to_pydantic_models: in 0.8.2 it writes each SHORTEN name into a Python declaration as it is, so a name with a hyphen (legal in an IRI) gives code that does not parse, and it makes every property a required field, so an instance without an optional property (sh:minCount 0) is refused (both found on the library model in the review of 2026-10-25). The ontology stays the source: regenerate the file after each release, and never edit the model to change the graph. Two of the server's tools stay unused. Its OWL import and export are lossy by its own README ("OWL Classes become Nodes, ObjectProperties become Relationships, and DatatypeProperties become Node properties"), and on 2026-10-24 load_from_owl_turtle rejected a released SKOS module whose object property has rdfs:domain skos:Concept, because that file does not declare skos:Concept an owl:Class. Its GraphRAG schema export is skipped, because this skill builds no extraction pipeline.

M. Release records#

One :ModuleRelease node per released module, in the local Neo4j and every copy. It says what the graph holds without bringing the catalog into the graph (multi-store.md, "What each store holds"). run_projection.py runs it in its release-record step and again on the copy target; files mode skips it, because plain files have no catalog.ttl.

uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 release_record.py records --report projection-report.json --manifest run-manifest.json --output release-records.json <package.ttl>...
NEO4J_PASSWORD=... uv run --no-project --with rdflib --with neo4j python3 release_record.py write --records release-records.json --uri bolt://127.0.0.1:<port>
NEO4J_PASSWORD=... uv run --no-project --with rdflib --with neo4j python3 release_record.py check --records release-records.json --uri bolt://127.0.0.1:<port>
FieldComes from
ontology, version_iriThe package file's owl:Ontology and its owl:versionIRI
module, versioncatalog.ttl's dcat:Dataset of that version IRI: the last part of its dcterms:isVersionOf, which must equal the ontology, and its owl:versionInfo
download_urlThe dcat:downloadURL in catalog.ttl that names the package file
conforms, in_graph_constraints, violationsThe projection report. They describe the whole load, because the shapes run over every module together
shapes_sha256SHA-256 of the release's shapes.ttl
projection_versionThe report's versions.method: the rules that loaded the graph
loaded_atThe time records ran, in UTC. The copy target gets the same value
  • It leaves the proved graph alone. The node has no :Resource label, and its link, (:ModuleRelease)-[:DESCRIBES]->(:Resource) to the module's owl:Ontology node, starts outside :Resource, so the graph hash, the counts, the module tags and the round trip read neither. write proves it: it writes nothing unless the graph hash equals the report's, and fails if the hash moves. No field enters any hash.
  • A report that did not earn its pass makes no record (build.report_earned, as add-on I). Nor does a package, shapes or catalog file whose SHA-256 is not in the run's run-manifest.json, so a record cannot describe a file edited after the load.
  • write is one transaction. A record with no owl:Ontology node, a moved hash or an error rolls it back, and the earlier records stay.
  • A load or a copy_graph.py --replace removes the records, as it removes any other non-:Resource graph, so the driver writes them after each.

To read them: MATCH (r:ModuleRelease)-[:DESCRIBES]->(o) RETURN r.module, r.version, r.conforms, r.violations, r.loaded_at, o.uri ORDER BY r.module.

Reviewing the loaded graph#

model_review.py checks a loaded graph (after step 6, or on the copy of add-on I) against the anti-patterns of Neo4j's neo4j-modeling-skill 1.0.7 that a projection keeps, with that skill's severities (ERROR a correctness failure, WARNING a performance or extensibility risk, INFO a style point):

NEO4J_PASSWORD="$PASSWORD" uv run --no-project --with rdflib --with neo4j python3 model_review.py \
  --uri "bolt://127.0.0.1:$PORT" [--report model-review.json] [--separator _]
uv run --no-project --with rdflib --with neo4j python3 model_review.py --env <target.env> [--report ...] [--separator _]
  • ERROR missing-key-constraint: no uniqueness or node-key constraint on :Resource(uri) (--key-label, --key-property for another key). n10s MERGEs on uri, and without the constraint it creates duplicates without a word.
  • WARNING generic-label and generic-type: a label whose local name is Entity, Node or Thing, or a relationship type whose local name is RELATED_TO, HAS or CONNECTED_TO, in any case and with or without _ or -. The fix belongs in the ontology: a more specific class or property.
  • WARNING supernode: a node with more than --max-degree relationships (default 100,000, the skill's limit). WARNING supernode-candidate: a node at --factor (10) times the median degree of one of its labels and at least --min-degree (50). Degree counts both directions. Concept schemes and widely used code-list values land here by design: read them against the ontology, and keep them as nodes (design-rules.md, "Where this skill departs from neo4j-modeling-skill").
  • INFO reciprocal-type, a local heuristic and not one of the skill's rules: one relationship type used from label A to B and from B to A. In a projection it usually means the ontology states one property in both directions where it meant a property and its inverse; the skill asks only that direction carry meaning.

Only domain labels count: n10s's own (Resource, the configuration labels, the schema labels, n4sch__* under n10s's names) are left out before every degree rule, and a node with none is not reviewed. When the load renamed the graph's names (pipeline.md, rule 11), give the same --separator: it splits each local name for the generic-name rules and names the schema labels every Cypher analysis leaves out; without it a renamed n4sch_Class node counts as a domain node and a generic lib_Entity goes unseen. The medians, offenders and reciprocal pairs are computed in Cypher, so only label statistics and at most --limit offenders (default 100) come back; the output says when the limit was reached. Every statement carries a server-side timeout, --query-timeout seconds (default 120). It exits 1 when it finds an ERROR, 0 otherwise, and 2 on bad input, a failed or timed-out query, or a report it could not write (the report is written by a rename, so an earlier one survives a failed write). No password or credential-bearing URI is printed: every error prints a fixed context and the exception's type, never its text (shell.error_line); the same holds for copy_graph.py, load_verify.py and triplestore.py. Fix an ERROR before the graph is used; read every WARNING against the ontology, which stays the master copy.

Anti-patterns#

Each is a way the projection passes while being wrong.

  • Relying on n10s defaults: overwrite for multivalued properties, invented ns0 prefixes.
  • Loading shapes the engine cannot run, and reading its silence as a pass.
  • Loading the reasoner's OWL API declarations as inferences.
  • Blank-node qualified-relation nodes or reifiers: the node or relationship then has no stable identity.
  • Merging two reifiers of one triple into one relationship.
  • Cypher written by hand rather than generated from the ontology.
  • Projecting working source files instead of released packages.
  • An exception list that is never checked for stale entries.
  • Expecting Neo4j to do OWL reasoning.
  • Treating Neo4j as the master copy instead of the Turtle files.
  • Trusting a shapes file to say what the engine checks: read back listShapes() and test every row (pipeline.md, rules 13 and 14).

Multi-store: one source, several stores, nothing lost#

From references/multi-store.md

Read it when the same released ontology must live in triple stores and in more than one Neo4j, and you must prove each copy holds exactly the source. It is the plan the skill's owner decided on 2026-10-23. Hops 1, 4 and 5 run with this skill's scripts, and hops 2 and 3 (skolemize, Jena Fuseki and the Databricks table, each with a no-loss round trip) with the rdf-store skill's. Hop 6, the rebuild, runs with run_projection.py (run-config.md), which also runs every other hop from one run configuration.

The flow#

HopWhat happensThe checkStatus
1. SourceThe released packages and their data files are the master copy (inputs.md, rule 1).check_projection_rules.py and validate_data.py pass (SKILL.md steps 2 and 3).Built
2. 3. Triple storesLoad the skolemized files into each store, one named graph per file. Any SPARQL 1.1 store through add-on J. Databricks through add-on K, from a notebook's Spark session: a Delta table in Unity Catalog with the columns subject, predicate, object, object_kind, datatype, lang, graph (object_kind says whether the object is an IRI, a blank node or a literal; rdf-store's references/stores.md has the table).The rdf-store round trip: export everything the store holds and compare it with the source by RDFC-1.0 hash; equal hashes mean zero lost and zero added. Counts per graph and per predicate are a quick look (triplestore.py adds the three-way counts against the n10s export).Built in the rdf-store skill; its README gives the tested runs

6. RebuildEmpty the local Neo4j and the copy. Rebuild both, taking a store's export (the Jena Fuseki dataset) as the source of hops 4 and 5.The rebuilt graph's hash equals the hash from hop 4, and its round trip against the original source files loses and adds nothing. That proves source → store → Neo4j → copy loses nothing.Built: run_projection.py, step rebuild (run-config.md)

What each store holds: the projection policy#

A released package has three graphs: <module>.ttl (the content), shapes.ttl (the rules) and catalog.ttl (the DCAT release record). The stores treat them differently, because they do different work.

StoreContent (<module>.ttl)Rules (shapes.ttl)Release record (catalog.ttl)
Triple store (Jena) and Delta tableAll, one named graphAll, one named graphAll, one named graph
Neo4j, local and the copyAll, with no selectionNot nodes. They validate the release: pySHACL before the load, n10s in the graph at the loadNot in full: one :ModuleRelease node per module (add-on M)
  • All the content, always. Do not project part of a module. The round trip's proof of 0 lost and 0 added compares the graph with the files, so a selective projection would lose that proof. A consumer that needs less of the graph filters it with labels or module tags (add-on F).
  • The rules run; they are not data. Shapes loaded as nodes would mix the rules with the things they describe, and the hash and the round trip would have to read around them. n10s keeps its compiled form of them in its own configuration, outside :Resource.
  • One record per release, not the catalog. A reader of the graph needs to know which release it holds and whether it passed. The rest of the catalog stays in the triple stores and the files.
  • One local Neo4j and one standing triple store. Keep one local graph, in one form, and copy that form to the other server: two local graphs in two forms give two sets of counts, and no reader can tell which is right. The run starts and stops no server, so it leaves the local graph, the copy and the jena dataset loaded and proven.

The data flow, box by box#

The diagram is diagrams/data-flow.png (source diagrams/data-flow.eraser; the editable diagrams/data-flow.excalidraw comes from diagrams/make_data_flow.py). Its groups, left to right, and every arrow:

Sources (grey, three boxes: "Source documents", "Industry and peer sources", "Reference process model"). They stand for the sources the ontology is built from, whatever the domain. Arrows into "W3C stack": the source material crosses into the ontology build; the ontology skill cites every fact it takes. Nothing here is checked by this skill.

Ontology build (ontology skill, Steps 1-11) (blue). "W3C stack: RDF, OWL, SKOS, SHACL, PROV-O, DCAT" → "check.sh, pySHACL, competency questions (SPARQL)" → "Released packages + DCAT catalog (git tags)". These are the ontology skill's steps; its gates prove each release before this skill reads it. The released packages are the master copy (hop 1 above).

Released packages → "Skolemize blank nodes (stable IRIs)" (yellow). What crosses: every released data file. What happens: hop 2. The check: no blank node left, and a second run writes the same bytes. Built in the rdf-store skill (rdfstore.py skolemize).

Skolemize → Triple stores (purple), two arrows:

  • "load, export back, compare" into "Apache Jena Fuseki, Graph Store Protocol, one named graph per package": the rdf-store skill publishes the graphs in one SPARQL Update request (--update, advised) or, without it, with one non-atomic PUT per graph, exports everything the store holds and compares it with the files by RDFC-1.0 hash. Built; triplestore.py (add-on J) adds the counts against the n10s export.
  • "triple for triple" into "Databricks: Delta triple table in Unity Catalog": add-on K, with the box under it, "Written and read by a notebook's own Spark session" (see "Databricks: Spark in a notebook" below). Built in the rdf-store skill, with the same round trip through a staging table.

Skolemize → ontology-to-lpg skill (orange): "Check: design rules, data shapes, refusals" → "Reason: ROBOT + ELK, once, upstream" → "Serialise: loadable.nt + inferred.nt (check-serialised)". What crosses: the released data files, or the skolemized copies hop 2 writes with the rdf-store skill when a consumer needs stable IRIs for blank nodes; both are built. They are SKILL.md steps 2 to 4, checks V1 to V5 below.

Serialise → Neo4j, local (n10s + APOC) (green): "n10s load (SHORTEN, fixed order), triples sent in the request" → "Gate: n10s listShapes() readback, one fail case per compiled constraint, round trip, determinism hash". What crosses: loadable.nt, inferred.nt, merged.ttl and the import-safe shapes, sent over Bolt in the requests of load_verify.py. The checks are V6 to V12 below. Built.

Jena ⇢ Gate, "three-way counts (--projection-report): files, store, Neo4j" (dashed): triplestore.py --projection-report <projection-report.json> compares the store's per-predicate counts with the files' and with the report's export_predicate_counts (check V14). Built.

Gate → Neo4j, another server (no plugins), "validated graph": "Copy over the driver to a named database; hash must match the local graph" → "GRAPH TYPE: schema enforced by the database". copy_graph.py (add-on I) copies the graph that passed V12 (check V13); build.py graph-type --output graph-type.cypher (add-on H) writes the statement applied after it (G1 to G4). Built.

Jena ⇢ Rebuild test ⇢ Check (dashed, red group): "Empty the local Neo4j and the copy, rebuild both from the Jena export, compare with the released files: no loss end to end". What crosses: the store's export, written by rdf-store's export as N-Quads and, with --ttl-dir, one Turtle file per graph, which re-enters the skill at "Check" and runs the whole path again; the check is hop 6, built as run_projection.py's rebuild step.

Released packages ⇢ Later: Unity Catalog (dashed): "OntoBricks (Databricks Labs): link Unity Catalog tables and metric views (the KPIs) to the business processes in the ontology". What crosses: the released ontology, as OntoBricks' domain ontology. No no-loss check applies: OntoBricks builds instances from tables, not from the release. Later, not part of this skill.

The validation path, V1 to V14, and GRAPH TYPE, G1 to G4#

The diagram is diagrams/validation-path.png (source diagrams/validation-path.eraser; diagrams/validation-path.excalidraw from diagrams/make_validation_path.py). Each check must pass before the next runs, in the order of the tables (the order SKILL.md steps 2 to 6 run them). The rules named here hold the detail; this section is the map. "Stops" means the command exits 1 (2 on bad input) and you go no further; from V6 to V12 it also means no report: load_verify.py writes projection-report.json only when every check passed (V12).

#WhatRule
G1build.py graph-type --output graph-type.cypher writes one CYPHER 25 ALTER CURRENT GRAPH TYPE SET statement from the sh:targetClass shapes and the data (list types follow the load's multivalued list; no empty node type), with what it leaves out as quoted // left out: commentsadd-ons.md, H

It covers labels, property types, NOT NULL (when sh:minCount is at least 1, list or scalar), lists (exactly the load's multivalued properties) and relationship endpoints. It leaves out relationship counts, sh:in, sh:pattern, ranges and lengths, which have no GRAPH TYPE form. Coverage depends on sh:targetClass shapes: a shape that targets by node or by SHACL-SPARQL gives no element type (on one multi-module test ontology, 35 node and 46 relationship element types). It guards later writes; the n10s gate (V6 to V12) stays the proof that the projection is right.

Why each step is there#

  • Skolemize first. Blank nodes have no identity outside one file: "Blank nodes do not have identifiers in the RDF abstract syntax" (RDF 1.1 Concepts, §3.5, https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf11-concepts/#section-skolemization). Each store would relabel them, so no consumer could point at one. (The rdf-store round trip still compares stores that hold blank nodes, through RDFC-1.0 canonicalization.) §3.5 allows systems to "replace some or all of the blank nodes in an RDF graph with IRIs" (quoted), and says Skolem IRIs meant to be recognised outside the system "SHOULD use a well-known IRI ... with the registered name genid", a path starting /.well-known/genid/ (quoted). Mint them under a base you document, such as https://id.example.org/.well-known/genid/, from a hash of the graph IRI and the blank node's RDFC-1.0 label, as rdf-store's skolemize does, so a rerun mints the same IRIs. Design rule 3 (design-rules.md) already keeps blank nodes out of the data; the files still hold them in OWL axioms and RDF lists, and those are what skolemizing fixes for the stores. A Skolem IRI minted from the node's RDFC-1.0 label is not an IRI "generated per run", which rule 3 forbids: the same input always gives the same IRI.
  • Export back, not only count. Matching counts can hide a changed value; the RDFC-1.0 hash of the export against the source's cannot (rdf-store).
  • Neo4j stays the projection. The triple stores hold the same triples as the source; Neo4j holds the projection that n10s, the shapes and the round trip verified. The rebuild of hop 6 tests that a store's copy is a valid source for the projection.

Databricks: Spark in a notebook#

The rdf-store skill builds add-on K (its references/stores.md). Spark is the only Databricks path: a notebook's own Spark session writes and reads the Delta table, so the load needs no host name, no warehouse and no credential. The release files reach the notebook from a volume or the workspace's files. The no-loss check is the same as for any store: the rows go through a staging table, and only a copy with the release's RDFC-1.0 hash replaces the live table.

Neo4j is loaded from the release files on your machine, never from the workspace: a graph written from a notebook would skip the local n10s gate.

  • No built-in triple store. Add-on K is a plain Delta table, written and read with SQL, and checked like any store in hop 3.
  • OntoBricks is a later tool, not the store. OntoBricks (Databricks Labs, https://github.com/databrickslabs/ontobricks, read at commit 97b27c7) works per domain: an ontology, R2RML mappings from Unity Catalog tables, and a graph it materialises from those tables. It builds instances only from the tables through the mappings, so it cannot hold the released files triple for triple. Use it later to link Unity Catalog data and metric views to the ontology.

Sharing a store with data that is not the ontology#

A project may want other graphs beside the projection in the same Neo4j database, such as a technical graph of its own pipeline (tables, steps, checks) that links to the ontology's measures and systems by IRI. Keep the projection's numbers untouched:

  • Its own label, never :Resource. The graph hash reads :Resource nodes and the edges between them (pipeline.md, rule 17), and the round trip exports :Resource nodes and the edges out of them (load_verify.py). Give every other node a label of its own and no :Resource label, and start every edge at one of its nodes, so no edge leaves an ontology node for it and neither number can see it. Then loading it moves none of those numbers: in a real project (2026-10-29) the graph hash, 4,193 nodes and the relationship counts were the same before and after a 134-node technical graph was loaded beside the ontology.
  • Pin the exact queries, not a pattern. Test that the functions computing the counts, the hash and the round trip send exactly the :Resource-only Cypher you expect: run them against a fake session that records each query and compare the strings. A regex scan of every query in the projection code looked like a stronger check but kept missing reads (a path variable, a label disjunction, parentheses inside a string literal); the project replaced it with the exact pin and claimed only what the pin covers.
  • A reload wipes it. load_verify.py starts each load with MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n, and copy_graph.py --replace empties the target first, so reload the other graph after every projection reload or copy.
  • Build it from the project's files. SPARQL Anything (https://sparql-anything.cc/, v1.3.0) turns SQL files, run commands, JSON and CSV into RDF with SPARQL queries kept beside the code, so the technical graph, or a decision trail written as PROV-O, comes from what the project already holds. If you type its records as prov:Activity, see the ontology playbook's PROV-O note on run shapes.

Keeping the stores in step#

The released Turtle is the master copy, held in Git where there is Git; every store is a copy that can fall behind it. Three kinds of copy need keeping in step, each by its own check: the ontology's triples in each store, a graph kept beside them, and files a release reads from outside Git.

The ontology's triples in each store#

Once several stores hold the projection, each can fall behind the newest release. In a real project (2026-10-29) this took these parts:

  • A marker per store. Each store records the release set it was loaded from (the catalog's datasets and the projection's input fingerprint): a node with its own label in each Neo4j, never :Resource, and a row in a table beside the triple table. The marker is written only after the store is checked against the repository: the pipeline's graph must give the committed report's hash and counts, the other Neo4j stores must hold the projection's nodes and relationships, the triple table must hold every module's newest release.
  • A standing triple store needs no marker. Its named graphs are version IRIs, so the store itself says which releases it holds: compare its graph names and each graph's triple count with the release files. That puts nothing extra in the store, so a later export compares equal to the files without an exclusion. A Fuseki started with --mem (the documented start) empties on restart, and the check then reads empty; reload it with run_projection.py --only jena.
  • A drift check compares each marker with the repository's newest catalog and each store's live count with its marker, and reports each store as current, behind, changed, unmarked or unreachable (with the error's name). It exits non-zero unless every store is current.
  • A sync reloads only what is not current, with the existing pipeline and driver rather than new loaders: local stores by default, cloud stores on request. It then reloads anything else the store held (see the section above) and marks what it reloaded.
  • A workflow on release tags reloads the cloud stores, and stays inactive until its logins exist as repository secrets: its first step checks them and every later step runs only if that check found them all. GitHub says "Secrets cannot be directly referenced in if: conditionals" and gives a job-level environment variable, tested in if, as its way round that (GitHub, "Using secrets in GitHub Actions", https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets, read 2026-10-29); a first step whose output later steps test is another way, and the one the real project used. Pin the checkout of any repository it runs code from.
  • A release step when nothing schedules it. Where no workflow runs the drift check, it is a written step of every release, and the ontology skill's references/release.md, "Keeping copies in step", says when it runs and which release the sync loads.

A graph kept beside the triples#

A graph that is not the ontology's triples, such as a technical or lineage graph (the section above) or a logical data model loaded as its own subgraph apart from the :Resource nodes, is loaded from its own files, so the release set cannot say whether it is current. Check it against those files:

  • Its own marker, written with the load. A node with its own label records a SHA-256 digest of the files the graph was loaded from (each file's name and hash, sorted). Write it in the same transaction as the load, so a marker never describes a load that failed.
  • A content fingerprint, not only counts. The check computes a fingerprint of what the store holds (each node's labels and key properties, each edge's type and the keys at its two ends, sorted, then hashed) and the same fingerprint from the files. A hand edit that leaves the counts unchanged then reads as changed.
  • A copy refreshed only from a matching source. A copy of the graph in another store, such as a lakehouse table read from Neo4j, is refreshed from its source store only when that source's fingerprint matches the files; otherwise reload the source first. A copy taken from a drifted source would carry the drift with a fresh date.
  • The previous graph or none, never part of one. Each load deletes the old graph and writes the new one, marker included, in one transaction, or loads beside it under a staging label and swaps once the load is complete. A failed load then leaves the graph that was there before.

Files a release reads from outside Git#

A file kept outside Git, such as an export a client keeps private, has no store marker: its path relative to its folder and its SHA-256, in the release's input record (release-inputs.json), are the record. The rules are the ontology skill's (references/release.md, "Inputs kept outside Git").

Versions of the method#

From references/versions.md

Read it when a project pins an earlier version of the guideline, or asks what changed. Each version keeps the earlier rules unless a line below says otherwise.

What 2.3 adds over 2.2#

From the projection of a multi-module enterprise ontology, every released package at once, in October 2026:

  1. The guideline becomes this skill. Repositories that kept a copy of 2.2 point here instead. The examples move to the library domain.
  2. Inputs are released packages (inputs.md, rules 1 and 2): each at its newest version, pinned by hand and checked against the release folder, each with its own shapes, plus the whole-graph shapes.
  3. The rules cover every namespace you own whose terms are predicates or classes, each with a fixed prefix, and the standard namespaces are registered too (inputs.md, rules 3 and 4).
  4. Release exceptions are a mechanism, not a checklist line (inputs.md, rules 5 and 6): keyed by the checker's exact message, each with its fix, failing on a stale entry. scripts/check_projection_rules.py implements it.
  5. Rule 4a counts an inverse link as an end and requires exactly one such link per node (design-rules.md, rule 4). Every qualified-relation class is registered with its ends.
  6. sh:pattern and literal sh:in lists leave the graph, found by testing n10s 2025.06.1 against the source (pipeline.md, rule 13); sh:in lists of IRIs stay. At first each constraint kind was tested in the engine with a pass and a fail case, and scripts/in_graph_shapes.py generated a subset; item 24 replaced both: every compiled row now gets its own case, and the gate is the engine's readback.
  7. Rule 1 and Rule 2 say how annotation properties and lists are stated: an annotation property needs a kind and a cardinality but no range; an optional list says sh:minCount 0.
  8. Rule 3 says why prefixes matter in SHORTEN mode: n10s names a term by its namespace's prefix and invents a numbered prefix for an unknown namespace.
  9. Running the projection (running.md): CI runs check and serialise only; the report's fingerprints cover every shape file; inferred.nt, the manifest and the report are committed together. (How the database was started and removed changed in item 25.)
  10. Scripts for the check, reason and serialise steps (load and verify followed in item 15): validate_data.py (pySHACL and the refusals) and build.py (the reasoner's merged input, the N-Triples files, the inferred filter, the generated load script, the manifest and the report check), with the jar checksums.
  11. Exact definitions where 2.2 left room: the byte sort order and the input fingerprint (pipeline.md, rule 5); the decimal and language-tag refusals (rule 3); which predicates load as arrays (rule 10); which file onto.import reads and what success is for the shapes import (rule 11); the export query and the schema rows it must leave out (rule 16); emptying the database between loads on Community edition (rule 17).
  12. Fixes found by running 2.3 end to end: ROBOT needs --include-indirect true to infer anything an individual's direct type does not already say (rule 4); array sorting is restricted to :Resource nodes, because sorting n10s's own configuration nodes corrupts them (rule 10); the export returns a tagged literal's text with literalLang set (rule 16).
  13. The in-graph subset follows the n10s source: it also drops sh:datatype values n10s throws on, sh:and, sh:or, sh:xone and a literal sh:hasValue, and keeps a property shape a targeted shape still uses (rule 13). Rule 14 gives a fail case for each constraint kind left in the graph. (Replaced by item 24.)
  14. The checker is stricter: a datatype range must be a row of the XSD to Cypher table; a cardinality counts only on an applied shape; every namespace a class uses needs a prefix; each qualified-relation end needs an exact shape; release exceptions waive only Rule 1, 2 and 5 gaps; the Rule 4 option and its reason are read from the configuration.
  15. A load-and-verify script, load_verify.py, from two more test runs (one on the library example, one on a private multi-module ontology): it loads with status checks, compares the shapes import with listShapes(), commits and restores the mutant, diffs the export with schema rows left out, and compares two hashed loads, with the hash fully specified. Its first fail cases were one per constraint kind, with kinds left without a case listed; item 24 replaced that with one case per compiled row.
  16. A round-trip fix: n10s exports a tagged string that holds a newline as xsd:string "text@en" with no literalLang; the diff now splits the tag with a DOTALL pattern (pipeline.md, rule 16).
  17. Rule 2 counts every target kind SHACL applies, and shapes reached through sh:node, sh:and, sh:or and sh:xone; it checks only the properties the data uses. Release-exception keys may use full IRIs.
  18. The in-graph subset keeps only the SHACL terms n10s reads, so sh:lessThan, sh:lessThanOrEquals, sh:equals and the like are dropped, as are IRI-named SHACL-SPARQL nodes and deactivated shapes. (Replaced by item 24.)
  19. Running details: the manifest records paths relative to its own folder. (The details of starting the database were replaced by item 25.)

Where 2.3 differs from the method as practised#

  • Annotation properties need no range here. The build behind 2.3 required a single range for every owned predicate, annotation properties included; this skill follows the ontology skill, where an annotation property takes neither a domain nor a range.
  • Rule 2 checks only properties the data uses. The build did the same; the first draft of 2.3 also checked declared but unused ones.
  1. From a later review (the subset parts replaced by item 24): the in-graph subset then ran n10s's own shape queries with rdflib (item 24 made that an advisory prediction); every script stops under Rule 4b; predicates inside property paths and superproperties need a prefix; a pin must be X.Y.Z. The manual cases and listed kinds this round introduced were removed by item 24.
  1. From the fourth quick check (replaced by item 24): this round made drop reasons name only the conditions that failed, and added a node-level sh:class kind, the carry-over of hand cases between runs and a <report>.previous file for a failed run. Item 24 removed the kinds, the carry-over and the .previous file.
  1. From the final run on a real multi-module ontology: build.py check-serialised checks the step 4 gate; the shapes list is built from the configuration's pins; own_namespaces needs only namespaces whose terms are predicates or classes; the pipeline's sections carry SKILL.md's step numbers.
  1. From quick check 6: check-serialised rejects lines that are not one triple and inferences already asserted, and runs in CI; printed commands are shell-quoted. Its rules on kinds, kinds_without_case, carried hand cases and reports set aside as invalidated were removed by item 24.
  1. The engine is the gate (replaces the subset rules of items 13, 18, 20 and 21, and the carried and set-aside reports of items 21 and 23). in_graph_shapes.py now leaves out only what makes n10s throw or judge valid data wrong, including value terms on an inverse path, which n10s checks the wrong way; its prediction of the compiled rows is advisory. load_verify.py reads listShapes() back after the import, compares it with the shapes file by target, path, param and value, and reports every constraint n10s did not compile (pipeline.md, rule 13). It plans one fail case per compiled row; each case creates its own node, so it needs no matching data, and passes only on its focus, path and component (rule 14). A row without a generated case fails the run until --manual-cases gives one; nothing is carried between runs (kinds_without_case, manual_cases, the carry-over and .previous are gone). The report is fail-closed: it is written, by a rename, only when every check passed, and check-report requires passed: true (running.md, rule 3). check-serialised accepts a line only when it is exactly one N-Triples triple, without comments. Add-ons H (GRAPH TYPE), I (copy to another Neo4j) and J (a SPARQL 1.1 triple store) are new; J was run on Jena Fuseki 6.2.0. references/multi-store.md records the plan for one release in several stores, with add-on K (Databricks). From the full review of the redesign: copy_graph.py copies only a graph whose hash equals a passing report's (--report, add-on I); every printed value is shell-quoted; a closed shape's compiled ignore-list must equal the file's; minimums are tested one value short; the store report is fail-closed like the projection report; the graph hash writes a date with its type; GRAPH TYPE takes its list types from the load's multivalued list and writes no empty node type; check-report requires a case for every compiled row. From the second review: every printed value goes through scripts/shell.py (a test reads every script's syntax tree), and build.py cypher and graph-type write to --output; check-report fails when compiled is missing; copy_graph.py and triplestore.py recheck a report with build.report_earned instead of trusting passed; a closed shape's ignore-lists must match the compiled rows both ways. From quick check 10: the print check is strict (every positional and keyword argument of every print or stdout/stderr write, no exemptions, and the three line-building helpers checked by the same rule); copy_graph.py compares the two databases by their db.info() id; pipeline.md rule 5 writes the manifest after check-serialised and the second SHACL run.

The scripts run against servers that already run: a local Neo4j 2025.06.2 with n10s and APOC, such as a Neo4j Desktop DBMS, named by an env file (running.md, rule 5), and Jena Fuseki started with Java from the plain Apache jar. check_plugins.py checks the two plugin jars by SHA-256 (running.md, rule 2). The load script's imports are n10s's import.inline procedures: the ontology and the shapes go in one request each, loadable.nt and inferred.nt in batches of whole lines, and the triples loaded must add up to each file's lines (pipeline.md, rules 8 and 11). load_verify.py takes --env or --bolt and an optional --database. copy_graph.py takes --source-env, --source-database and --target-database, and copies to a named database on a server with no plugin (add-on I). run_projection.py takes neo4j_env, plugins_dir, and a dataset URL for jena, explore_fuseki and triplestore_fuseki; it empties each dataset before it loads, and its steps no longer include a Databricks round trip, which runs in a notebook through the rdf-store skill's SparkStore. The method's rules and its report are unchanged, and a graph loaded this way has the hash the earlier load gave.

Migrating a project from 2.2#

Expect the checker to report two things a 2.2 project did not see:

  • A missing xsd: prefix. Rule 3 now counts datatype ranges, so the namespace of every rdfs:range datatype needs a prefix in the configuration.
  • A stale release exception on an annotation property. 2.2 builds required a range on annotation properties too; 2.3 does not, so an exception listed for an annotation property with no range no longer occurs and fails as stale. Remove it.

Learning path: the W3C skills a clean projection needs#

From references/learning-path.md

Read it when the user asks what to learn before modelling for a property graph, or asks for practice exercises. Thirteen skills in priority order: ★★★ is needed for the five design rules, ★★ is important, ★ is good to know. About six to eight weeks at a few hours a week. Exercises use the library example in design-rules.md.

#SkillPrioritySupports
1RDF data model and IRIs (triple terms for Rule 4b)★★★Rules 3, 4
2Turtle and N-Triples (reifier syntax for Rule 4b)★★★Rule 4; serialise
3RDFS: classes, properties, domain and range★★★Rule 1
4OWL 2: property kinds, the EL profile, reasoning★★★Rule 1; reason
5XSD datatypes and literals★★★Rule 1; the type table
6SHACL Core★★★Rule 2; check; verify
7SPARQL (CONSTRUCT; triple terms for Rule 4b)★★serialise
8Modelling patterns: n-ary relations, qualified relations, reification★★Rule 4
9SKOS for taxonomies and labels★★add-on B
10Standard vocabularies: QUDT, PROV-O, OWL-Time★add-ons E, F
11Canonicalisation and graph comparison★verify
12Neo4j modelling and n10s★★★load
13Research background: S3PG and PG-Schema★Rules 1, 2; add-on H

What to master, with one exercise each#

  1. RDF and IRIs. The four kinds of term (IRI, literal, blank node and, in RDF 1.2, triple term, allowed only as an object); asserting a triple against only reifying it; why blank nodes break determinism. Exercise: model one work with two authorships (author, then illustrator) as two qualified-relation nodes, and explain why the graph gets two :lib_Authorship nodes. Sources: RDF 1.2 Primer and Concepts; W3C "Cool URIs for the Semantic Web".
  2. Turtle and N-Triples. Prefixes, the ; and , shorthands, typed and tagged literals; for 4b, <<( s p o )>>, ~ reifier and {| ... |}. Exercise: write the authorship in Turtle, convert it to sorted N-Triples, and confirm the sorted file does not change between runs. Sources: RDF 1.2 Turtle and N-Triples; Jena RIOT.
  3. RDFS. rdfs:domain and rdfs:range infer types; they do not restrict. Use SHACL to restrict. Exercise: give lib:copyOf the domain lib:Copy and predict what a reasoner infers for a subject that is not typed as a copy. Source: RDF Schema.
  4. OWL 2. The three property kinds (Rule 1); classes and named individuals; property characteristics the graph does not enforce; open world against closed world; the EL profile and ELK. Exercise: reason over the library module with ROBOT and ELK, and build inferred.nt by the set difference in pipeline.md, rule 6. Sources: OWL 2 Primer and Profiles; ROBOT reason.
  5. XSD. Lexical form against value ("01"^^xsd:integer equals "1"^^xsd:integer); timezones; decimal precision against float; language tags. Exercise: write a shape that rejects an xsd:dateTime without a timezone. Sources: XML Schema 1.1 Part 2; the Cypher Manual's values and types.
  6. SHACL. Node and property shapes, sh:targetClass, the cardinality, datatype, class, node-kind, sh:in and sh:pattern constraints; reports and severities; which constraints n10s runs (pipeline.md, rule 13). Exercise: write the authorship shape (an IRI, exactly one agent, exactly one inverse link from a work) and make it fail once on purpose. Sources: SHACL; pySHACL; Validating RDF Data (Labra Gayo and others).
  7. SPARQL. SELECT, CONSTRUCT, ASK, FILTER, OPTIONAL, EXISTS, BIND; for 4b, SUBJECT(), PREDICATE(), OBJECT(), isTRIPLE(). Exercise: derive the direct edge work lib:createdBy person from the authorship nodes with one CONSTRUCT. Sources: SPARQL 1.1 and 1.2 Query.
  8. Modelling patterns. The test in design-rules.md, rule 4: a link with its own identity or lifecycle is a domain class; a link that only carries facts is a Rule 4 case. Exercise: model a loan both as a qualified relation between a member and a copy and as a lib:Loan domain class, and write down why fines and renewals need the class. Source: W3C Note "Defining N-ary Relations on the Semantic Web".
  9. SKOS. Concepts, schemes, preferred and alternative labels, broader and narrower, mappings; when a term is a concept and when a class. Sources: SKOS Primer and Reference.
  10. Standard vocabularies. QUDT for units, PROV-O for provenance, OWL-Time for validity periods; search Linked Open Vocabularies before inventing a term.
  11. Comparison. RDF Dataset Canonicalization (RDFC-1.0); rdflib to_isomorphic and graph_diff. Exercise: diff a graph against itself after a shuffle and get an empty result.
  12. Neo4j and n10s. Labels, relationship types, properties and constraints; n10s configuration, import, validation and export; APOC's apoc.merge.relationship and apoc.coll.sort. Exercise: run the load and verify steps end to end on the library module. Sources: Neo4j GraphAcademy (data modeling and Cypher fundamentals); the neosemantics documentation.
  13. Research background. S3PG (Kashif Rabbani, Matteo Lissandrini, Angela Bonifati and Katja Hose, "Transforming RDF Graphs to Property Graphs using Standardized Schemas", Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data 2(6), article 242, December 2024, https://doi.org/10.1145/3698817) converts RDF graphs to property graphs driven by their SHACL shapes, emitting PG-Schema, and reports lossless transformation where other methods lose query answers. PG-Schema (Renzo Angles and others, "PG-Schema: Schemas for Property Graphs", Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data 1(2), article 198, June 2023, https://doi.org/10.1145/3589778) proposes a schema language for property graphs, motivated, as its abstract says, by the ISO standardisation of GQL; Cypher 25's GRAPH TYPE (add-on H) states a subset of the same ideas. Neither is a tool this skill runs: read them for why shapes, not the OWL axioms, decide value against relationship (Rules 1 and 2), and for what add-on H's GRAPH TYPE can and cannot state. Exercise: write by hand the PG-Schema node type for lib:Copy from its shapes and compare it with what build.py graph-type prints.

Flashcards#

  • A literal object becomes? A node property. An IRI object? A relationship.
  • Two qualified-relation nodes for one link (4a) give how many graph nodes? Two. Two reifiers of one triple (4b) give how many relationships? Two.
  • Which SHACL property decides one value or an array? sh:maxCount.
  • Why must qualified-relation nodes and reifiers be IRIs? The IRI becomes the stable uri in the graph.
  • What does Neo4j not do that OWL needs? Open-world reasoning.
  • How does n10s match sh:pattern? Against the whole string, so anchor every pattern and check patterns before the load.

End of the Ontology-to-LPG projection playbook. Built from ../README.md, design-rules.md, inputs.md, pipeline.md, running.md, run-config.md, add-ons.md, multi-store.md, versions.md, learning-path.md.
